summary:
SpectraBlink is a single-file, interactive web app that explains NASA’s SPHEREx mission, an infrared space telescope launched on 11 March 2025. It maps the whole sky in 102 narrow infrared colours (0.75–5.0 µm), giving every point on the sky its own spectrum.

The app has six tabs:

The mission: key stats, a first all-sky map video, a chart comparing SPHEREx’s 102 bands with WISE’s four broad filters, the science goals (cosmic inflation, galaxy history, ices as ingredients of life) and a data timeline.
Latest news: mission updates up to Data Release 1 (12 Nov 2026), with links to the original NASA and Caltech pages.
Sky atlas: a zoomable, pannable all-sky infrared map from NASA’s WISE telescope, with several views.
Colour lab: splits the maps into their three infrared bands so you can reassign colours and adjust gains.
Compare: flips between two images (Blink), reveals one over the other (Swipe) or highlights changes (Difference). You can also upload your own images.
Gallery: five WISE sky views with a lightbox.

It’s built as one 13 MB HTML file with embedded images, and the polished version adds the styling and usability improvements I described.
details:
Each tab does a different job. Together they take you from understanding the mission to exploring and experimenting with the data.

The mission

This is the explainer page. It opens with a short plain-language summary of what SPHEREx is, then a video of the first all-sky map. Below that are eight stat cards (102 bands, resolving power, pixel size, four sky passes, launch date, data volume, images per day, archive delay), each with a short note on what the number means. A chart compares SPHEREx’s 102 narrow bands with WISE’s four broad filters on a log wavelength axis. It also marks where water ice, PAH, CO₂ ice and CO ice absorb light. The page ends with three science goals (cosmic inflation, galaxy history, ices as the ingredients of life) and a dated timeline from launch to Data Release 1.

Latest news

This is a dated feed of mission news from the last 18 months, newest first. The Data Release 1 item is highlighted and tagged “NEW”. It covers the brown dwarf spectra, the “interstellar glaciers” ice maps, the comet 3I/ATLAS observations and the awards. Each item links to the original NASA, JPL or Caltech page, and a note says when the news was last checked.

Sky atlas

This is the main viewer for real WISE all-sky infrared maps. You pick one of the views from a row of thumbnails, then pan by dragging and zoom with scroll or pinch. There are also +, − and reset buttons. A colour legend explains the map: red is 22 µm warm dust, green is 4.6 µm and blue is 3.4 µm starlight. The Hide outlines checkbox removes the red and yellow outline markers that were drawn on the exported images. The app does this by filling those pixels in from their surroundings. Two collapsible notes explain what the outlines probably are.

Colour lab

Infrared light has no natural colour, so this tab lets you choose the colours yourself. Each source map is really three greyscale images stacked, one per WISE band. The lab separates them and shows the three bands as small panels. You can then send any band to the red, green or blue display channel. Sliders adjust each channel’s gain and a brightness (gamma) boost, and presets give you quick starting points. The large canvas updates live. It shows how scientists turn invisible light into false-colour images.

Compare

This tab is for spotting differences between two images. SPHEREx will map the sky four times, and this is the same idea used to find things that moved or brightened. You pick Image A and Image B (and can swap them), then choose a mode:

Blink flips between the two at an adjustable speed, so changes seem to jump.

Swipe puts a divider you can drag across the frame to reveal one image over the other.

Difference subtracts the images pixel by pixel. Black means identical and bright blue means different, with a sensitivity slider.

You can also use quick-comparison presets and upload your own images, which are fitted into the same frame. A full-screen button enlarges the stage. A collapsible guide has an apparent-speed slider that suggests whether something is a star, a nearby mover or an asteroid-like object.

Gallery

Five WISE all-sky views appear as cards with a title and short description. Clicking one opens a full-size lightbox. You can step through images with the on-screen arrows or the left and right arrow keys, and close with Escape or the × button.
